summary: Extends the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol so a client can ask a PCE to avoid certain things when computing a route. These are constraints that the client sets as exclusions in MPLS and GMPLS networks.

plainLanguage.summary:
A path computation element works out a route through a network when a client asks it to. This RFC lets the client say which parts of the network that route must leave out, so the element can find a path around them.

The client can mark an exclusion as a hard rule or as a preference, and can apply a rule to the whole route or to a single hop of a route it has spelled out itself.

questions: how to exclude routes in pcep
what is the pcep exclude route object
how to exclude nodes in pcep
what is an exclude route object
subtitle: How a path computation client tells a path computation element which parts of the network to avoid.

tldr.problem: A Path Computation Client that asks a Path Computation Element for a route sometimes needs that route to leave out particular resources, but the PCEP protocol had no way to say so.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an Exclude Route Object that a client attaches to a path computation request, listing resources to leave out, and a new Explicit Exclusion Route subobject for exclusions that apply only to one hop of a route the client spells out itself.
tldr.outcome: Exclusions can now be mandatory or best-effort, and a server can report which exclusions blocked a path. The document is a Proposed Standard and builds on the PCEP protocol defined in RFC 5440.

today: RFC 5521 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It adds route exclusions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol defined in RFC 5440, so a deployment needs that protocol as well as these extensions. The document itself notes that the security measures of RFC 5440 become more important with these extensions, not less.

sections.title: Why a Client Asks for Exclusions
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes a network path from a graph of the network, applying constraints that the requester supplies. A Path Computation Client (PCC) asks for a path by sending it a request, and the PCE returns the path it computed.

Sometimes the client needs a path that avoids particular resources. A backup path for inter-domain label switched paths, for example, must share no nodes, links or shared risk link groups (SRLGs) with the working path. A network operator may also want a path to avoid nodes that are about to be taken out of service for administrative reasons.

The requirement to support route exclusions was already stated in the generic requirements for the PCEP protocol. What was missing was a way to express them on the wire, which is what this document adds to PCEP, the protocol defined in RFC 5440.
sections.plainLanguage: A path computation element works out a route through a network when a client asks it to. This RFC lets the client say which parts of the network the route must not use, so the element can find a path around them.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Route Exclusion
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes two kinds of route exclusion, both taken from the RSVP-TE extensions in RFC 4874.

  • Exclude Route List: the exclusion of abstract nodes or resources from the whole path. This list is carried in a new PCEP object, the Exclude Route Object (XRO).
  • Explicit Route Exclusion: the exclusion of abstract nodes or resources between one specific pair of abstract nodes named in an explicit route. This is carried by a new subobject of the existing Include Route Object (IRO), called the Explicit Exclusion Route subobject (EXRS).

The XRO is optional and may travel in a Path Computation Request and in a Path Computation Reply. In a request it lists the resources the PCE is asked to leave out. In a reply that reports a failure it can name the exclusions that made a path impossible, and in a reply that reports success it can carry exclusions that the client should signal to the network while setting the path up.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to say no. One keeps a resource out of the whole route. The other keeps it out of a single hop between two named points in a route that is otherwise spelled out.

sections.title: The Exclude Route Object
sections.content:
The XRO body starts with a 16-bit Reserved field, which MUST be set to zero on transmission and SHOULD be ignored on receipt, and a 16-bit Flags field. The only flag defined is the F (Fail) bit, which sits at bit 15 of the field. When the F bit is set, the request asks for a new path for an existing traffic engineering label switched path that has failed, and the request MUST also carry the path of that failed label switched path in a Record Route Object. That lets the computation take the previous path and its reserved resources into account, so it does not book the same bandwidth twice when the traffic engineering database has not caught up or the resources have not yet been released.

The rest of the body is one or more subobjects. An XRO with no subobjects MUST NOT be sent and SHOULD be ignored on receipt. Each subobject carries an X bit that says whether the exclusion is mandatory or only desired. With the X bit clear, the resource MUST be excluded from the computed path. With the X bit set, the resource SHOULD be excluded but MAY be used if no path meeting the other constraints of the request exists.

The XRO Object-Class is 17 and the XRO Object-Type is 1.
sections.plainLanguage: The XRO is an optional box that travels with the request. It has a small fixed header and then a list of entries, each naming something to keep out of the route. Each entry also says whether keeping it out is a hard rule or a preference.

sections.title: XRO Subobjects and Their Fields
sections.content:
Every XRO subobject starts with the X bit and a 7-bit Type field, followed by a Length field that counts the whole subobject, including the Type and Length fields themselves. Five subobject types are defined: type 1 for an IPv4 prefix, type 2 for an IPv6 prefix, type 4 for an unnumbered interface identifier, type 32 for an autonomous system number and type 34 for a shared risk link group. The IANA registry also lists type 64 for a Path-Key with a 32-bit PCE identifier and type 65 for a Path-Key with a 128-bit PCE identifier.

Where a subobject carries an address, a Prefix Length field says how many bits of that address are significant. If the subobject names a single address, the prefix length MUST be set to the full length of the address.

The Attribute field says how the PCE should read the subobject. The value 0 means the subobject names interfaces, the value 1 means it names nodes, and the value 2 means it names shared risk link groups, in which case resources that share a risk group with the named ones are excluded as well. The RFC limits the first two values to particular subobject types and allows the third for every subobject. For a shared risk link group subobject the Attribute SHOULD be set to two and SHOULD be ignored on receipt.

The shared risk link group identifier is four bytes long. The autonomous system number subobject carries a two-octet AS number, and the RFC notes that, as in other PCEP and RSVP-TE objects, no support for four-octet AS numbers is provided.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry names a kind of network resource: an IPv4 or IPv6 address, an interface, an autonomous system, or a group of links that fail together. A second field says whether to read the entry as an interface, a node or a risk group.

sections.title: How a PCE Handles an Exclude Route Object
sections.content:
When a PCC builds an XRO it clears the X bit for each exclusion that must be honoured and sets it for each exclusion that is only desired, and it sets the Attribute field of every subobject.

When a PCE receives a request it looks for an XRO. If it finds more than one, it MUST use the first one in the message and MUST ignore the later ones. If it does not recognise the XRO, it MUST return an error message with the Error-Type "Unknown Object". If it is unwilling or unable to process the XRO, it MUST return an error message with the Error-Type "Not supported object".

If the PCE does compute a path, it MUST honour the exclusions exactly as they were expressed. The returned path MUST NOT include any resource encoded with the X bit clear, and SHOULD NOT include any resource encoded with the X bit set unless alternative paths that match the other constraints in the request are unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: When the server finds an XRO it uses the first one in the message and follows it. If it does not understand the object at all, it says so with an error. If it does understand it, the path it returns must leave out everything that was marked as a hard rule.

sections.title: Explicit Route Exclusion
sections.content:
An Explicit Route Exclusion names the network elements that must not, or should not, be used on the path between two abstract nodes that the client has already named in the Include Route Object. It is encoded as a new Include Route Object subobject, the Explicit Exclusion Route subobject, with type 33. The EXRS holds one or more subobjects of its own, in the same format as the XRO subobjects, and the meanings of their fields do not change. Only the scope does, because the exclusion applies to the single hop between the previous and the next element of the include route.

An EXRS MUST NOT be sent with no subobjects, and one received with no subobjects MUST be ignored. A PCE that does not support EXRS treats the include route as a malformed object, and may include the include route in the error message, in which case the include route SHOULD be terminated immediately after the unrecognised EXRS.

A PCE that supports EXRS but meets a subobject it does not recognise MUST act on the X bit. With the bit clear it MUST respond with an error whose Error-Type is "Unrecognized EXRS subobject" and whose Error-Value is the EXRS subobject type code. With the bit set it MAY respond with that error or MAY ignore the subobject, which is a local policy decision. For a subobject it does recognise, the PCE MUST follow the requirement it carries: with the X bit clear it MUST NOT produce a path that uses the named resource between the previous and the next abstract node of the include route, and with the X bit set it SHOULD NOT produce such a path unless it cannot construct one that avoids the resource while still meeting the other constraints in the request.
sections.plainLanguage: When a client spells out part of the route itself, it can also say which resources to avoid between two named points. That is carried as a new entry inside the object that holds the spelled-out route.

sections.title: Excluding a Path That Is Kept Confidential
sections.content:
In inter-domain path computation the domains may belong to different service providers, so the topology of one domain may have to stay secret. In that case the working path is not spelled out in full: Path-Key subobjects, defined in RFC 5520, stand in for segments of the path, and the client receives an Explicit Route Object holding those Path-Keys instead of the real hops.

When the client then asks for a backup path that must be disjoint from the working path, it copies the whole working path into the XRO. If the working path was returned with Path-Key subobjects, those subobjects are copied too, so the PCE can still check diversity. The L bit of a Path-Key inside an XRO MUST be ignored.

The PCEs used for the backup computation may be the same ones used for the working path, or a different set. With the same PCEs, a PCE that meets a Path-Key in the XRO recognises itself from the PCE identifier in the Path-Key and converts it into a set of XRO subobjects for its own calculation; those subobjects MUST NOT be shared with other PCEs. With different PCEs, a PCE that meets a Path-Key sends a request to the PCE named in the Path-Key to expand it, and treats the returned segment as a set of XRO subobjects for its own calculation; those subobjects again MUST NOT be shared with other PCEs.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the first path is described in a shortened way because the network operator does not want to reveal its internal hops. The backup request copies that description, so the server can still check that the two paths do not overlap.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The exclusion mechanisms give finer control over the path a PCE computes, and that raises the stakes if a PCEP message is intercepted, modified or spoofed, because an attacker could then steer the computed path or make the computation impossible. The security techniques described in RFC 5440 are therefore more important, not less. The RFC also notes the other side of the coin, that the same mechanisms let an operator route around vulnerable parts of the network.

On management, a MIB module for PCEP is being specified in a separate document. That module MUST be extended so that an operator can examine the route exclusion extensions defined here. Two local policy choices at the PCE are called out. The exact behaviour when a desired exclusion cannot be met SHOULD be available for examination by an operator and MAY be configurable. The behaviour on receipt of an unrecognised XRO or EXRS subobject with the X bit set SHOULD be configurable and MUST be available for inspection.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever can change a request to the server can change the route it returns, so the protections of the base protocol matter more here, not less. The same feature also lets an operator steer traffic away from parts of the network that are known to be weak.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: MUST be set to zero on transmission and SHOULD be ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: 16 bits. The F (Fail) bit is bit 15 of the field. Other bits are unused.

fields.name: X
fields.desc: 0 means the resource MUST be excluded; 1 means it SHOULD be excluded but MAY be used if no path exists.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Subobject type. 1 for an IPv4 prefix.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the subobject including the Type and Length fields.

fields.name: IPv4 address
fields.desc: The IPv4 address, or the first address of the prefix.

fields.name: Prefix Length
fields.desc: How many bits of the address are significant. The full length for a single address.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.desc: How to read the subobject: 0 Interface, 1 Node, 2 SRLG.

items.desc: An IPv6 address or prefix to be excluded.

items.desc: An unnumbered interface, named by TE Router ID and Interface ID.

items.label: SRLG

viz.caption: THE FOUR THINGS AN EXCLUSION CAN SAY

items.title: Exclude Route List
items.text: Keeps a resource out of the whole computed path. Carried in the XRO.

items.title: Explicit Route Exclusion
items.text: Keeps a resource out of one hop of a route the client spelled out. Carried in the EXRS.

items.title: X bit clear
items.text: The resource MUST be excluded from the computed path.

items.title: X bit set
items.text: The resource SHOULD be excluded, but MAY be used if no other path exists.
